# Clouds Against Humanity

A small, cheap, locked-down DigitalOcean environment built with OpenTofu, applied by Spacelift, fed secrets by Doppler, and reachable only through Twingate. **No droplet has a single public inbound port open.** There is no VPN, no bastion host and no SSH on the internet.

It is a cloud extension of a homelab, and it exists to teach: this repository is the reference environment, and the lessons that use it live in the wiki.

> ### Start with the wiki
>
> **The wiki is the real point of this project.** Every lesson, flowchart, exercise and decision (including the ones that were wrong the first time) is written there; this repository is the environment those lessons use.
>
> - **[Wiki home](https://github.com/ChiefGyk3D/Clouds-Against-Humanity/wiki)**: the map of everything.
> - **[Start here if you are new](https://github.com/ChiefGyk3D/Clouds-Against-Humanity/wiki/Start-Here-If-You-Are-New)**: cloud, Terraform and zero trust from zero.
> - **[Why this exists](https://github.com/ChiefGyk3D/Clouds-Against-Humanity/wiki/Why-This-Exists)**: where this comes from and who it is for.
> - **[Reading order](https://github.com/ChiefGyk3D/Clouds-Against-Humanity/wiki/Reading-Order)**: the paths, with time estimates.
> - **[Contents](https://github.com/ChiefGyk3D/Clouds-Against-Humanity/wiki/Contents)**: every page once, grouped by theme, with what each is for.
> - **[Git from zero](https://github.com/ChiefGyk3D/Clouds-Against-Humanity/wiki/Git-From-Zero)**: if you have never used git.
> - **[Repository growth](https://github.com/ChiefGyk3D/Clouds-Against-Humanity/wiki/Repository-Growth)**: stars, forks and weekly work, drawn from GitHub data; the as-of date is printed in the picture, and stars measure attention, not use.
>
> **Who this assumes:** a basic power user. You know how a computer works, may have built or repaired one, and have set up a router and done basic networking. If you could work a help desk or a retail repair counter, you can start; if not, [IT 101 level material such as CompTIA A+ objectives](https://github.com/ChiefGyk3D/Clouds-Against-Humanity/wiki/Start-Here-If-You-Are-New#where-zero-is) is the benchmark (not an endorsement).
>
> **Cost:** the reading and the exercises are free and always will be, and nothing here is sold. Hands-on work uses your own accounts and your provider's bill, nothing you spend goes to the maintainer, and you choose what you can afford to run. The cost gates are explained in [docs/cost.md](docs/cost.md). If you open a DigitalOcean account, my [referral link](https://m.do.co/c/e3aaa65aed6b) is optional and nothing is gated behind it; the wiki says exactly what it is. The same pages are in [`docs/wiki/`](docs/wiki/Home.md) if you prefer reading them in the repo.

> ### Found a mistake or have a question? Open an issue
>
> Something wrong, a command that failed, a confusing explanation, or a topic you wish was here? Please say so. Feedback is free, and it is how the lessons get better. **[Give feedback and open an issue](https://github.com/ChiefGyk3D/Clouds-Against-Humanity/wiki/Give-Feedback-and-Open-an-Issue)** walks through it for a first-timer. Never paste tokens, keys, account names, real IP addresses or hostnames, or anything that identifies you. Security problems go through [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md), not a public issue. See also [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md).

## Free, and not for sale

I grew up in a divorced home, struggling to find resources to level up my tech knowledge, and my whole career was built on second hand machines. My first brand new computer, a System76 Pangolin I still have, came roughly ten years in. If knowledge is power and getting to it costs money, then the power is only available to people who can afford it, and I refuse to be selfish and enrich myself by gatekeeping what everyone has a right to know. No bullshit, no "90K in 90 days" lies, no "you need this cert or degree." Just knowledge.

You can tip, donate or support me financially through [Patreon](https://patreon.com/chiefgyk3d), [StreamElements](https://streamelements.com/chiefgyk3d/tip) or the [cryptocurrency section](#cryptocurrency-tips), but you are under no obligation. The biggest way to support this project is to share it with everyone who needs it. The full version, including what I think of college and certs, is [Why this is free and not for sale](https://github.com/ChiefGyk3D/Clouds-Against-Humanity/wiki/Why-This-Exists#why-this-is-free-and-not-for-sale).

Recommending other springboards is encouraged throughout this project. The point is to get you thinking in different ways and outside the box, not to hand you one path to copy, so expect pages to point at things to try beyond what they cover.

| Piece | Job | Why this and not the obvious alternative |
|---|---|---|
| **Twingate** (ZTNA) | Gets an authenticated person to one specific host and port | Connectors dial out, so nothing listens on the internet. A VPN would mean a public listener and network-wide access after one login. [More](docs/wiki/Why-ZTNA-Not-a-VPN.md) |
| **DigitalOcean** | Droplets, VPC, cloud firewalls | Predictable pricing and a firewall that attaches by tag, so a droplet is protected from its first boot. [More](docs/wiki/DigitalOcean-Network-and-Firewalls.md) |
| **OpenTofu** | Every resource as code, in layered stacks | Open-source (MPL) Terraform fork; same language, no license surprise. [More](docs/wiki/OpenTofu-Stacks-and-Modules.md) |
| **Spacelift** | Runs plan and apply, holds state, waits for a human | Nothing applies from a laptop or from CI, and pull request plans never see credentials. [More](docs/wiki/Spacelift.md) |
| **Doppler** | Holds every secret | Spacelift holds one read-only token; nothing in this repo is a credential. [More](docs/wiki/Doppler-and-Secrets.md) |
| **GitHub Actions** | Tests, scanners, cost gate | Calls hardened shared workflows, every action pinned by commit. [More](docs/wiki/CI-Tests-and-Cost-Gate.md) |

## Why not just a VPN?

Because a remote-access VPN authenticates you once and then puts your device on the network, and the box doing that authentication has to listen on the internet. Both halves of that have been the starting point of serious breaches: stolen credentials on a legacy single-factor VPN profile (Colonial Pipeline, 2021) and a long run of pre-authentication exploits in VPN appliances from Ivanti, Fortinet, Palo Alto, Citrix and Pulse Secure. ZTNA checks every connection against a per-resource policy and, as built here, leaves nothing listening at all.

That is not "VPNs are always wrong". WireGuard is a very different animal from an SSL VPN appliance, site-to-site tunnels are still fine, and ZTNA means trusting a vendor's control plane. The full argument, sources and the honest tradeoffs are on **[Why ZTNA and not a VPN](docs/wiki/Why-ZTNA-Not-a-VPN.md)**.

# CloudGoat 2.0 is here!

CloudGoat is Rhino Security Labs' "Vulnerable by Design" cloud deployment tool. It allows you to hone your cloud cybersecurity skills by creating and completing several "capture-the-flag" style scenarios. Each scenario is composed of cloud resources arranged together to create a structured learning experience. Some scenarios are easy, some are hard, and many offer multiple paths to victory. As the attacker, it is your mission to explore the environment, identify vulnerabilities, and exploit your way to the scenario's goal(s).

Below are our main goals for CloudGoat:

* **Focused, Curated, High-Quality Learning Experiences** - Each of CloudGoat’s scenarios should provide the opportunity for experimentation, exploration, and building hands-on cloud security skills.
* **Good Documentation** - We've done our best to ensure that CloudGoat’s scenarios are well-documented and easy to understand and evaluate in terms of difficulty, content, structure, and skills-required.
* **Easy to Install and Use** - We understand that CloudGoat is a means to an end - learning and practicing cloud security penetration testing. Therefore, we aim to keep things simple, straightforward, and reliable.
* **Modularity** - Each scenario is a standalone learning environment with a clear goal (or set of goals), and CloudGoat is able to start up, reset, or shut down each scenario independently.
* **Expandability** - CloudGoat’s core components (python app and scenarios) are designed to permit easy and independent expansion - by us or the community.

Before you proceed, please take note of these warnings!

> **Warning #1:** CloudGoat creates intentionally vulnerable resources into your account. DO NOT deploy CloudGoat in a production environment or alongside any sensitive resources.

> **Warning #2:** CloudGoat can only manage resources it creates. If you create any resources yourself in the course of a scenario, you should remove them manually before running the `destroy` command.

## Requirements

* Linux or MacOS. Windows is not officially supported.
  * Argument tab-completion requires bash 4.2+ (Linux, or OSX with some difficulty).
* Python3.9+ is required.
* Terraform >= 1.5.0 [installed and in your $PATH](https://learn.hashicorp.com/terraform/getting-started/install.html).
* The AWS CLI [installed and in your $PATH](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cli/latest/userguide/cli-chap-install.html), and an AWS account with sufficient privileges to create and destroy resources.
* The AZ CLI [installed and in your $PATH](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cli/azure/install-azure-cli#install), and an Azure account with sufficient privileges to create and destroy resources.
* [jq](https://stedolan.github.io/jq/)

Linux
```bash
sudo apt install terraform awscli azure-cli jq -y
```

Mac
```bash
brew install terraform awscli azure-cli jq
```

## Quick Start

To install CloudGoat, make sure your system meets the requirements above, and then run the following commands:

```bash
pipx install cloudgoat
```
You may also want to run some quick configuration commands - it'll save you some time later:

Configure for AWS - tell CloudGoat which AWS profile to use.
```bash
cloudgoat config aws
```
Configure for Azure - tell CloudGoat which Azure subscription to use.
```bash
cloudgoat config azure
```
Log in to Azure - CloudGoat uses the active `az` account.
```bash
az login
```

Configure whitelist
```bash
cloudgoat config whitelist --auto
```
Now, at your command, CloudGoat can `create` an instance of a scenario in the cloud. When the environment is ready, a new folder will be created in the project base directory named after the scenario and with a unique scenario ID appended. Inside this folder will be a file called `start.txt`, which will contain all of the resources you'll need to begin the scenario, though these are also printed to your console when the `create` command completes. Sometimes an SSH keypair named `cloudgoat`/`cloudgoat.pub` will be created as well.

> **Note:** Don't delete or modify the scenario instance folder or the files inside, as this could prevent CloudGoat from being able to manage your scenario's resources.

As you work through the scenario, feel free to refer to the scenario's readme if you need direction. If you get stuck, there are cheat sheets linked at the bottom of each route's walkthrough.

When you are finished with the scenario, delete any resources you created yourself (remember: CloudGoat can only manage resources it creates) and then run the `destroy` command. It's always a good idea to take a quick glance at your web-console afterwards - just in case something didn't get deleted.

You can read the full documentation for CloudGoat's commands [here in the Usage Guide section](#usage-guide).

## How to use CloudGoat's Docker image

[](http://play-with-docker.com?stack=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RhinoSecurityLabs/cloudgoat/master/docker_stack.yml)

### Option 1: Run with default entrypoint
```console
docker run -it rhinosecuritylabs/cloudgoat:latest
```

### Option 2: Run with AWS config and credentials

> Warning: Running this command will mount your local AWS configuration files into the Docker container when it is launched. This means that any user with access to the container will have access to your host computer's AWS credentials.

```console
docker run -it -v ~/.aws:/root/.aws/ rhinosecuritylabs/cloudgoat:latest
```

## Scenarios Available
(Grouped by Difficulty)

  Easy

---

### iam_enum_basics (Easy)
`cloudgoat create iam_enum_basics`

In this scenario, you start with the access keys for a low-level IAM user named Bob. Your task is to perform thorough IAM enumeration using the AWS CLI. By investigating managed policies, inline policies, group memberships, and assumable roles, you will uncover five distinct flags. 

[Visit Scenario Page.](cloudgoat/scenarios/aws/iam_enum_basics/README.md)  

Contributed by Tyler Ramsbey

---

### data_secrets (Easy)
`cloudgoat create data_secrets`

In this scenario, you start with an IAM user with limited permissions. Your task is to identify a misconfigured EC2 instance leaking credentials in its User Data, allowing you to gain SSH access. From there, you must pivot by exploiting the Instance Metadata Service (IMDS) to steal a role, enumerate Lambda functions to find hidden environment variables, and finally compromise a user with access to the scenario's objective: a secret stored in AWS Secrets Manager.

[Visit Scenario Page.](cloudgoat/scenarios/aws/data_secrets/README.md)  

Contributed by Tyler Ramsbey

---

### beanstalk_secrets (Easy)
`cloudgoat create beanstalk_secrets`

In this scenario, you are provided with low-privileged AWS credentials that grant limited access to Elastic Beanstalk. Your task is to enumerate the Elastic Beanstalk environment and discover misconfigured environment variables containing secondary credentials. Using these secondary credentials, you can enumerate IAM permissions to eventually create an access key for an administrator user. With these admin privileges, you retrieve the final flag stored in AWS Secrets Manager.

[Visit Scenario Page.](cloudgoat/scenarios/aws/beanstalk_secrets/README.md)  

Contributed by Tyler Ramsbey

---

### sns_secrets (Easy)
`cloudgoat create sns_secrets`

In this scenario, you start with basic access to an AWS account. You need to enumerate your privileges, discover an SNS Topic you can subscribe to, retrieve a leaked API Key, and finally use the API Key to access an API Gateway for the final flag.  

[Visit Scenario Page.](cloudgoat/scenarios/aws/sns_secrets/README.md)  

Contributed by Tyler Ramsbey

---

### iam_privesc_by_key_rotation (Easy)
`cloudgoat create iam_privesc_by_key_rotation`

Exploit insecure IAM permissions to escalate your access. Start with a role that manages other users' credentials and find a weakness in the setup to access the "admin" role. Using the admin role, retrieve the flag from Secrets Manager.

[Visit Scenario Page.](cloudgoat/scenarios/aws/iam_privesc_by_key_rotation/README.md)

Contributed by Infrasec.sh

### iam_privesc_by_rollback (Easy)
`cloudgoat create iam_privesc_by_rollback`

Starting with a highly-limited IAM user, the attacker is able to review previous IAM policy versions and restore one which allows full admin privileges, resulting in a privilege escalation exploit.

[Visit Scenario Page.](cloudgoat/scenarios/aws/iam_privesc_by_rollback/README.md)

---

### lambda_privesc (Easy)
`cloudgoat create lambda_privesc`

Starting as the IAM user Chris, the attacker discovers that they can assume a role that has full Lambda access and pass role permissions. The attacker can then perform privilege escalation using these new permissions to obtain full admin privileges.

> **Note:** This scenario may require you to create some AWS resources, and because CloudGoat can only manage resources it creates, you should remove them manually before running `./cloudgoat destroy`.

[Visit Scenario Page.](cloudgoat/scenarios/aws/lambda_privesc/README.md)

### sqs_flag_shop (Easy)
`cloudgoat create sqs_flag_shop`

First, start with the SHOP page where you can buy FLAG. The website has a number of pages, and you can see that the source code is exposed. Attackers analyze the code to find vulnerabilities and use their privileges to purchase FLAG.

[Visit Scenario Page.](cloudgoat/scenarios/aws/sqs_flag_shop/README.md)

### static (Medium)
`cloudgoat create static`

In this scenario, you act as an external attacker visiting a corporate portal. By analyzing the web application, you identify that it loads critical JavaScript libraries from a public S3 bucket. You must discover a misconfiguration in the bucket's permissions, perform a "Supply Chain Attack" by overwriting the library with malicious code, and wait for an internal administrator bot to log in. Your goal is to capture the bot's credentials and exfiltrate them back to the bucket.

[Visit Scenario Page.](cloudgoat/scenarios/aws/static/README.md)  

### vulnerable_cognito (Medium)
`cloudgoat create vulnerable_cognito`

In this scenario, you are presented with a signup and login page with AWS Cognito in the backend. You need to bypass restrictions and exploit misconfigurations in Amazon Cognito in order to elevate your privileges and get Cognito Identity Pool credentials.

[Visit Scenario Page.](cloudgoat/scenarios/aws/vulnerable_cognito/README.md)

Contributed by TrustOnCloud

`cloudgoat create vulnerable_lambda`

In this scenario, you start as the 'bilbo' user. You will assume a role with more privileges, discover a lambda function that applies policies to users, and exploit a vulnerability in the function to escalate the privileges of the bilbo user in order to search for secrets.  

[Visit Scenario Page.](cloudgoat/scenarios/aws/vulnerable_lambda/README.md)

`cloudgoat create cloud_breach_s3`

This page is for you if you have a Raspberry Pi or an old PC running a few things at home, you have heard words like "cloud", "Terraform", "zero trust" and "CI" without anyone ever explaining them, and this repository is one of your first looks at how infrastructure is built in a professional setting. Nothing on the start-from-zero pages assumes you have worked in IT. They assume you are curious and can type a command.

The rest of the wiki was written for people who already know the vocabulary. It is still the real documentation of this environment, and you will be able to read it by the time you finish these pages.

Where zero is

The zero this project presumes is a basic power user. You know how a computer works, you may have built or repaired one, and you have set up a router and done basic networking. If you are qualified for basic help desk or an entry-level IT position, even as someone working a retail or repair counter at a place like Micro Center or Geek Squad, you know enough to start here.

If that is not you yet, that is fine: look at IT 101 level material first, including but not limited to the objectives of CompTIA A+, which is the certification most commonly associated with the minimum I am looking for you to know. This is not an endorsement of CompTIA or of any exam. It is just the benchmark people recognize, and it was checked as a public page on 2026-10-22. The primers here (What is the cloud, Networking basics and Linux for enterprise beginners) are a bridge into the cloud and security side, not a substitute for knowing what a computer, a router or an IP address is.

What this project actually is, in plain words

If you want the reason behind the project before the detail, Why this exists is a short side page about that. It is not a step in the path below.

The author has a homelab: computers at home that run bots, dashboards and a security monitoring stack. This project rents two small computers from a cloud company (DigitalOcean), locks them down so that nothing on the internet can connect to them, and builds a private way to reach them. Later stages will move some of the home bots onto a third rented computer.

Everything about those rented computers is written down as code in this repository: what size they are, what network they sit on, which connections their firewall allows, which user may log in. A hosted service reads that code and builds the real thing. Changing the environment means changing the code, having it checked, and then approving the change. Nobody clicks around in a web console.

That is the whole idea. The rest is detail, and the detail is what the pages are for.

The mental model: homelab words to cloud words

Most cloud concepts have a homelab equivalent. Start from what you already have.

At home you have	In the cloud it is called	How it is different	Page
A Raspberry Pi or an old PC running Linux	A virtual machine; DigitalOcean calls one a droplet	Rented by the hour, created and destroyed with an API call, and it has a public internet address from the moment it boots	What is the cloud
Your home LAN behind the router	A VPC, virtual private cloud	A private network you define, with addresses you choose; nothing else in the datacenter is on it	Networking basics

Applying them builds it; tofu destroy (or removing a resource from the files and applying) tears it down. Deleting the files alone removes nothing, and the bill keeps coming	What is infrastructure as code

Following along

You can get something out of this repository at three levels of commitment.

Reading only, $0. Everything here is public, including the code, the tests and the decisions. You can run the tests on your own computer without any cloud account, because they use fake providers; the infrastructure as code page shows how.

Build stage 0, $0. Stage 0 creates a project, a private network and a firewall. None of those cost money at DigitalOcean. You need a DigitalOcean account, a Spacelift account and a Doppler account, all of which have free tiers at the time of writing (check their pricing pages; this repo does not promise they still do). The stage 0 guide is the step-by-step.

Build stage 1, $12 a month. Two small droplets with Twingate connectors. This is the first stage that costs money, and the first one you can SSH into. You also need a Twingate account. The stage 1 guide covers it, and the cost page says what to expect on the bill.

Whatever level you pick, read How money works in the cloud before you create an account, and set a billing alert before you create anything else.

How to read these pages
Words in bold on first use are defined in the Glossary.
A diagram is never the only explanation. If a flowchart does not land, the text under it says the same thing.
"Why" comes before "how" on purpose. If you understand why a firewall rule exists, you can write the next one. If you only know how, you can only copy.
Everything that was tried and failed is on Lessons learned. Read it as a list of things you are now allowed to skip.
Where a page states a vendor price, a limit or a product feature, it says the date it was checked. Those things change; the reasoning does not.
What this is not

It is not a tutorial that ends with a working website. The environment is deliberately tiny: two machines, zero open ports, one way in. The value is in how it was built and why, and in the fact that every decision, including the wrong ones, is written down. If you want to learn cloud by building a thing, pick a thing and build it; then come back here to learn how to build it so that it does not get owned, does not surprise you on the bill, and can be rebuilt from scratch in an afternoon.

On what I left out, and on AI

While this project helps you learn, some things have purposely been left out, condensed, or only given as partial lessons, because I, just like the real field, will not spoonfeed you all the answers, and AI can't reason for you. Learn to understand this yourself first, and then at most guide and direct the AI.

I will be honest and say I still google things the old-fashioned way, as you may call it today, because it is often faster and I can reason better than AI can. Practice it and you will get better at it. AI is a great tool, but it is not always right or perfect, and it will amplify what you are great at and what you suck at. Use it as a tool, not as a crutch.

I am not anti AI. Scrum Around and Find Out, Department of Internal Arguments, FrankenLLM, Stream Daemon, Boon Tube Daemon, Star Daemon, Penguin Overlord and Yo Mama as a Service all have various AI features, I run my own AI server, and I am in both the Anthropic and OpenAI cybersecurity programs.

If something here is wrong, confusing or does not work on your computer, please tell me: Give feedback and open an issue shows how, and it costs nothing.

Why this exists

Nothing to read first. This page is opinion, my own, and it says so. If a word is new, the Glossary defines it. For the tool choices specifically, Why I picked these tools goes piece by piece.

Home > Start here > Why this exists

Consider this my manifesto. The ramblings of a mad man.

I built this because I was sick of zero trust knowledge being locked behind the companies that sell it, where you can only find out how a ZTNA platform really works by paying for the platform and then sitting through a sales pitch while you do. Every vendor says they are the right answer, and Zero Trust is still poorly understood until you are inside an enterprise, so the people who most need to learn it (the ones who are not inside one yet) get the marketing version.

This is me distilling and condensing what I learned over almost four years of working with zero trust network access and enterprise networks, into something you can read for free and try in your own accounts.

Why this is free and not for sale

I grew up in a divorced home, struggling to find anything I could use to level up my tech knowledge. My whole career was built on second hand machines. I bought my first brand new computer, a System76 Pangolin I still have, roughly ten years into my career. Aside from desktops I have built from new here and there, about 90% of my PC collection is second hand.

Here is where that leaves me. If knowledge is power, and getting to the knowledge costs money, then the power is only available to people who can afford it. I have to be able to look in the mirror and be proud of myself, whether that is me today or the me from 15 years ago who needed these exact lessons.

So: no bullshit. No "90K in 90 days" lies, no "you need this cert or degree." Just knowledge.

I do not have a four-year degree, and I earned the CISSP about twelve years into my career. I am also in WGU, and I have seen first hand how bad it is. The Python class was laughably horrible: it taught bad habits and wrong approaches to version control, among other things. That is not an indictment of WGU, it is an indictment of college as a whole. Too many people think going to college for cybersecurity will be enough. It is not, and you will be horribly unprepared. I have seen it first hand, in the people coming in and the people around me. I have met people with master's degrees in cybersecurity who could not figure out how to open PowerShell, and went looking for it through the Okta tiles in their web browser. I wish I were joking.

So if you want to succeed, stop chasing the next cert or piece of paper and go after real knowledge. I hope some of you reading this get a wakeup call. The open source revolution is here, knowledge is power, and I refuse to be selfish and enrich myself by gatekeeping what everyone has a right to know.

You can tip, donate or support me financially in a few ways, through my content, cryptocurrency or Patreon, but you are under no obligation. The options are on the Home page. The biggest way to support this project is to share it with everyone who needs this knowledge to level up.

Where I am coming from

Zero trust took me around six months to learn, and that was with the advantage of administering Zscaler at work, with architects whiteboarding it for me and spending hours with me, plus a lot of documentation. But zero trust was only one piece. It took me around three years to get comfortable with Terraform, with the ways around an enterprise, with infrastructure as code, and with shifting everything left the way I do, which is pretty much everything this project talks about. I am not saying that was three years of full-time study, only that this is how long it took before it felt like mine.

If that is what it took with the real platform in front of me, a team around me and a job that required it, I do not think it is reasonable to expect anyone to piece it together alone from vendor pages.

So the point of this project is to let you shortcut years of head bashing. I will not promise you a timeline, because I do not know yours and I have not measured anyone's. What I can say is that the lessons are the part that cost me the most to find, written down so you can spend your time on the parts that teach you something instead of the walls.

I am not going to say more about my job than that. What I know about enterprise networks I know from doing it, and where I only know something from reading, the pages say so.

Why Twingate

If Zscaler were more affordable I might have used it here, and I say that from working with it every day. It is not, at least not for one person with a homelab, so I settled on Twingate, and I use it myself.

The reason that matters for this project is the connector. In both Twingate and Zscaler there is a node you deploy inside the network you want to reach, and it dials out, so you do not open an inbound port. That means it can sit in front of devices that cannot run an agent, such as IoT gear, and you reach them through it without building a jump host. In this repository the connectors are two small droplets, and Twingate and Why ZTNA and not a VPN show the rest.

Plenty of you will reach for Tailscale or something like it, and that is a fair choice, so here is the comparison as fairly as I can make it.

Question	Twingate	Zscaler (ZPA)	Tailscale
Reaching a device that cannot run the client	Deploy a connector next to it; it dials out.	The same idea: an App Connector. Not read from a vendor page, est.	A subnet router extends your tailnet to "devices that don't or can't run the Tailscale client" (Tailscale docs).
How access is described	Per resource, per group, set in the admin console or in code.	Per application segment, est.	Access rules over the tailnet, with a subnet router advertising routes.
What it costs a hobbyist	There is a free tier at the time of writing, est. (check the pricing page).	Sold to enterprises; I could not afford it for a lab.	There is a free personal plan, est. (check the pricing page).

I am not saying Tailscale is wrong. It also reaches devices that cannot run a client, and for plenty of homelabs it is the simpler tool. What pulled me toward Twingate was that its model (a connector, resources, groups, and per-resource policy) is the closest thing I could afford to what I work with in an enterprise, and the point of this project is to teach that model. If you use Tailscale and learn the ideas, you have lost nothing.

Disclosure: Twingate gave me a plan for free for a review. The free plan covers stages 0 and 1, and it has two gaps. My lab has an identity provider and uses SAML authentication, which the free plan does not include (on the free plan you sign in with social login instead). And stage 2's cloud-to-home paths use Twingate service accounts, which Twingate's pricing page lists on its Home, Business and Enterprise plans and not on the free Starter plan. The details are in Why I picked these tools and Twingate service accounts in CAH.

Sources, retrieved 2026-10-22: Twingate, Connectors ("Connectors are Twingate components that are deployed behind your firewall to provide access to private Resources", read directly). Tailscale, Subnet routers (quoted above, read directly). Zscaler's help pages (help.zscaler.com) returned only a JavaScript shell to a plain curl, so I could not read the App Connector text; the Zscaler cells are from my own work with it and marked est. The "no jump host" point is my own experience, not a sentence from the Twingate page. I did read Twingate's pricing page on 2026-10-22 for the disclosure above, but I did not read Tailscale's or Zscaler's, so nothing here should be taken as a price. On that page Twingate lists secure service accounts on the Home, Business and Enterprise plans and not on the free Starter plan. The stage 2 design uses a headless client, which needs a service account, so stage 2's cloud-to-home paths need a plan above Starter; Twingate service accounts in CAH has the sources, the one place Twingate's pages disagree, and what Twingate does not say.

Cost, and who pays for what

This project has cost gates. They exist and I will not pretend otherwise: a change that would push the planned monthly bill past the ceiling is refused. The ceiling for the current phase and the per-phase table are on the Roadmap, and the arithmetic and how to raise it are in docs/cost.md.

I would like to be plain about what that means, because it is not a paywall. The reading and the exercises are free and always will be, and every page is readable without an account. Hands-on work uses your own accounts and your own provider's bill (or hardware you already own or choose to buy), and nothing you spend goes to me. You decide what you can afford to run. The labs in Labs: break it on purpose need no cloud account and cost nothing. Going further is your call and your budget.

What I did not want was for you to depend on a CTF platform or some other subscription service to learn this, where the money flows to someone who is selling you access to the practice. Here you can run it yourself, in your own accounts, and tear it down when you are done, with a checklist that helps you verify no billable resources remain. Billing data lags, so the checklist has you look again the next day, and it does not promise a final bill of zero.

Free, and staying free

There is no paywall here, nothing is sold, and nothing in this project pays me. The lessons, the code and the wiki are free and stay free, under the Apache-2.0 license in the repository, and I refuse to gatekeep knowledge, which is half of why this exists.

My standing promise is that if I ever have an affiliation or sponsorship with something I recommend, I will disclose it as it appears, the way I did for Doppler. The disclosures that exist today are in Why I picked these tools: Doppler sponsored content I made years ago, Twingate gave me a plan for free in exchange for a review, and I have a DigitalOcean referral link that earns me credit if you use it and spend (it is optional, and the project is identical without it). Where the link appears the page says so.

There are optional support links in the Home page and the wiki footer, for people who want to support continued development. They are optional, and nothing in the wiki or the repository is gated behind them.

Who it is for

If you are a self-starter who can teach yourself, you will go a long way, and this is for you. I am not trying to hand you a certificate. I am trying to give you a springboard, the way I had to build mine, with some extra twists so you hit fewer walls than I did, and to point you at real field work and complex ideas and get you thinking outside the box.

A lot of what matters at work sits in places that college classes and certifications do not touch, and I have picked up much of it from colleagues across many disciplines. I believe a good share of it is not properly covered anywhere, at least not without the bullshit and the sales pitches attached, so some of these pages are me writing down what those people taught me. The ones that are my opinion say so.

The motto, and the method

You are not dead until you stop learning.

Question everything, on every piece, including these pages.
